concepts.title: Pods, Ephemeral Storage, and Why State Doesn't Belong There
concepts.description: A container's writable filesystem, and even a Pod's emptyDir scratch space, disappear the moment the Pod itself is replaced -- understanding exactly what survives a container restart versus a Pod replacement, and why hostPath only relocates the problem rather than solving it, is the gap that PersistentVolumes exist to close.
learningObjectives: Explain why a container's own writable filesystem layer is not a safe place to store data that must survive anything beyond that single container run.
Describe what happens to an emptyDir volume's contents when a container inside a Pod restarts, versus when the Pod itself is deleted, evicted, or rescheduled.
Explain why a hostPath volume ties a Pod's data to one specific node, and why that's a dangerous default for anything managed by a ReplicaSet or Deployment.
Distinguish workloads where losing all local state on replacement is acceptable (caches, scratch space, render buffers) from ones where it isn't (databases, message queues).
Explain, at a high level, why none of a container's writable layer, emptyDir, or hostPath actually solves the general 'storage that survives and follows a replaced Pod' problem.

sections.heading: A Container's Writable Layer Dies With the Container
sections.body:
Every running container has its own writable filesystem layer, stacked on top of the read-only image layers it was built from. It behaves like a normal filesystem from inside the container -- you can write a file to /data/cache.json and read it right back -- but that writable layer belongs to that one specific container instance, not to the Pod as a durable concept and not to the image.

This matters because of a detail that's easy to miss: when the kubelet restarts a crashed container **in place** (same Pod, governed by `restartPolicy`), it doesn't resume the old container process -- it starts a brand-new container instance from the same image, with a brand-new, empty writable layer. Anything written to the old container's writable layer, and never written anywhere else, is gone the moment that container exits, restart or not. This is precisely why `kubectl logs --previous` is a genuinely useful command and not just a curiosity -- the previous container's writable filesystem, including any log files it wrote to local disk instead of stdout, is already unreachable by the time you'd think to go looking for it.

```bash
kubectl exec app-pod -- sh -c 'echo cached > /data/cache.txt'
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /data/cache.txt
# cached

# container crashes and the kubelet restarts it in place...
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /data/cache.txt
# cat: /data/cache.txt: No such file or directory
```

The fix for this specific problem -- data that should survive a container restart within the same Pod -- is a **volume**, which is exactly what the rest of this concept is about. But it's worth being precise from the start about which volume types actually solve which scope of problem, because two of the most commonly reached-for ones only solve part of it.

sections.heading: emptyDir: Node-Local Scratch Space for the Pod's Lifetime
sections.body:
An `emptyDir` volume is a directory that Kubernetes creates on the node when the Pod is scheduled there, and mounts into any of the Pod's containers that ask for it. Unlike a container's own writable layer, an `emptyDir` volume is **Pod-scoped, not container-scoped** -- its contents survive an individual container restarting in place within the same Pod, which fixes the exact failure shown above, and it's also the standard mechanism for two containers in the same Pod to share files with each other on local disk (a log-writer and a log-shipper sidecar, for instance).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: cache
      emptyDir: {}
```

But the name is exact and worth taking seriously: it's tied to the **Pod's** lifetime, not to any single container's, and definitely not beyond the Pod's. The moment the Pod itself is deleted, evicted, or lost along with its node -- not a container restart, the whole Pod object going away -- the kubelet removes the `emptyDir` directory from the node entirely. A replacement Pod, even one created from an identical template by the same controller seconds later, gets a fresh, empty `emptyDir`; it does not inherit the previous Pod's directory, because from Kubernetes' point of view it's an entirely unrelated Pod object that merely looks similar.

One edge case worth knowing: `emptyDir` can be backed by `medium: Memory` (a tmpfs mount) instead of the node's real disk, useful for latency-sensitive scratch data -- but that memory usage counts against the Pod's memory limit, and the data is lost even faster: on any container restart involving a full Pod-level tmpfs remount, and certainly on a node reboot, since tmpfs never touches persistent disk at all.

sections.heading: hostPath: Real Disk, But Nailed to One Specific Node
sections.body:
A `hostPath` volume mounts a path from the **node's own filesystem** directly into a Pod's container -- real, persistent disk, not memory, and not deleted when the Pod is deleted.

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      hostPath:
        path: /var/lib/my-app-data
        type: DirectoryOrCreate
```

This looks, at first glance, like exactly the fix for the `emptyDir` problem above -- the data genuinely does survive Pod deletion. But it only survives **on that one node**. A Pod managed by a ReplicaSet or Deployment has no guarantee whatsoever of landing on the same node twice; the scheduler picks whichever node fits best at that moment, with zero awareness that 'this Pod's hostPath data lives specifically on node-3.' A rolling update, a node drain, or simply the scheduler's normal placement decisions can land the replacement Pod on node-7 instead, where `/var/lib/my-app-data` is a completely different, empty directory -- from the application's point of view, indistinguishable from having lost all its data, because for all practical purposes, it has.

This is precisely why `hostPath` is not a general storage solution -- it's a node-scoped escape hatch, appropriate mainly for workloads that are themselves inherently node-scoped by design (a DaemonSet reading that specific node's own log directory or Docker socket, for instance), not for anything a ReplicaSet is expected to freely reschedule across nodes. Using it for a database is a well-known, common mistake precisely because it *appears* to solve the durability problem in casual testing (restart the Pod on the same node a few times, data's still there) right up until a reschedule proves otherwise, often during exactly the kind of node failure the cluster was supposed to survive gracefully.

sections.heading: The Actual Gap: Storage That Outlives AND Follows the Pod
sections.body:
Line up what's needed against what these three options each provide: a container's writable layer survives nothing beyond that one container run; `emptyDir` survives a container restart but not a Pod replacement; `hostPath` survives a Pod replacement but only if the replacement happens to land back on the exact same node, which nothing guarantees.

What a database, a message queue, or any workload with data that must genuinely persist actually needs is storage that (1) survives the Pod being deleted and replaced, full stop, and (2) is reachable from wherever the replacement Pod happens to be scheduled, not tied to a specific node's local disk at all. None of the three mechanisms above provide both properties simultaneously -- and that's not an oversight in any of them; each is doing exactly what it's designed to do at its own intended scope. Getting both properties together requires storage that exists as its own independent resource, decoupled from any specific node, that a Pod can be handed regardless of where the scheduler places it -- which is exactly the abstraction PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims introduce, covered next.

examples.title: emptyDir Surviving a Container Restart, Then Disappearing on Pod Deletion
examples.code:
kubectl exec app-pod -- sh -c 'echo important > /data/state.txt'
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /data/state.txt
# important

# Simulate a container crash-and-restart within the SAME Pod:
kubectl exec app-pod -- sh -c 'kill 1'
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /data/state.txt
# important   -- still there; emptyDir is Pod-scoped, not container-scoped

# Now delete the Pod entirely (e.g. it's owned by a Deployment, so a replacement appears):
kubectl delete pod app-pod
kubectl get pods -l app=app-pod-label
# NAME              READY   STATUS
# app-pod-9f7x2      1/1   Running   -- a NEW Pod object

kubectl exec app-pod-9f7x2 -- cat /data/state.txt
# cat: /data/state.txt: No such file or directory
examples.explanation: The first `kill 1` inside the container simulates the main process crashing; the kubelet notices the container exited and restarts it in place, inside the *same* Pod, and the emptyDir directory -- which belongs to the Pod, not that specific container instance -- is untouched, so `state.txt` is still there. Deleting the Pod entirely is a fundamentally different event: the Pod object itself is gone, its emptyDir directory is removed from whichever node it was on, and the replacement Pod that a Deployment's ReplicaSet creates (`app-pod-9f7x2`, a new name) starts with a brand-new, empty emptyDir -- there is no 'previous Pod' relationship carried forward at all, even though the replacement was built from an identical template.

examples.title: hostPath Data Stranded on the Wrong Node After a Reschedule
examples.code:
kubectl get pod db-pod -o wide
# NAME     STATUS    NODE
# db-pod   Running   node-1

kubectl exec db-pod -- sh -c 'echo row1 >> /var/lib/db-data/data.log'

# node-1 is drained for maintenance; the Pod is evicted and rescheduled
kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

kubectl get pod db-pod -o wide
# NAME     STATUS    NODE
# db-pod   Running   node-3

kubectl exec db-pod -- cat /var/lib/db-data/data.log
# cat: /var/lib/db-data/data.log: No such file or directory
examples.explanation: The write to `/var/lib/db-data/data.log` genuinely persisted on node-1's real disk -- hostPath data isn't wiped by a container or even a Pod restart on that same node. But draining node-1 forces the Pod off it, and the replacement lands on node-3, whose own `/var/lib/db-data` directory has never had anything written to it. The application sees an empty file (or a missing one), with no error indicating data was 'lost' in any way it could detect -- it simply looks like a fresh start, because as far as this node's filesystem is concerned, that's exactly what it is. This is the specific, common failure mode that makes hostPath unsuitable for anything a scheduler is free to move around.

misconceptions.description: emptyDir volumes are wiped out whenever a container restarts, so they're only useful for data that survives within a single, uninterrupted container run.
misconceptions.clarification: It's the opposite of the risky case for emptyDir: the directory is scoped to the Pod, not to any individual container inside it, so it specifically survives a container crashing and being restarted in place by the kubelet -- that's exactly the scenario it's designed to protect against. What actually destroys an emptyDir volume is the Pod itself being deleted, evicted, or rescheduled -- a different, coarser-grained event than a container restart, and one that's easy to conflate with it if you haven't tested both cases separately.

misconceptions.description: Mounting a hostPath volume makes a Pod's data as durable as a real persistent disk, since it's written to the node's actual filesystem instead of an ephemeral container layer.
misconceptions.clarification: It is durable -- on that specific node. The problem isn't that hostPath data disappears the way emptyDir's does; it's that a Pod managed by a ReplicaSet or Deployment has no guaranteed relationship to any particular node at all, so a routine reschedule (a rolling update, a drain, a node failure) can land the replacement Pod anywhere else in the cluster, where that same hostPath refers to a completely different, empty directory. hostPath doesn't remove the 'data tied to one physical location' problem; it just moves that location from 'inside one specific Pod' to 'on one specific node,' which is still the wrong scope for anything the scheduler is free to relocate.

exercises.prompt: A Pod has a single container with an emptyDir volume mounted at /cache. The container writes a file, then the container process crashes and the kubelet restarts it. Later, someone runs `kubectl delete pod` and a Deployment's ReplicaSet creates a replacement. At which of these two points does the file at /cache/data.txt actually disappear, and why?
exercises.code:
kubectl exec cache-pod -- sh -c 'echo v1 > /cache/data.txt'
# container crashes, kubelet restarts it in place
kubectl exec cache-pod -- cat /cache/data.txt   # ?

kubectl delete pod cache-pod
# ReplicaSet creates a new Pod, cache-pod-7f2ab
kubectl exec cache-pod-7f2ab -- cat /cache/data.txt   # ?
hints: emptyDir is scoped to the Pod as a whole, not to any single container running inside it -- does a container restart change which Pod the volume belongs to?
Deleting the Pod is a different kind of event than a container crashing inside it -- what actually happens to the node-side directory backing an emptyDir volume when the Pod object itself is removed?
The replacement Pod has a different name. Is there any mechanism that would connect its emptyDir to the deleted Pod's emptyDir?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The file survives the container restart (still prints 'v1') because emptyDir belongs to the Pod, not the individual container. It disappears at the second point -- after `kubectl delete pod` -- because deleting the Pod removes its emptyDir directory from the node entirely, and the replacement Pod (a new, unrelated object) gets a brand-new, empty emptyDir with no connection to the deleted one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The container crash-and-restart is a Pod-internal event: the kubelet replaces the container process but the Pod object, and therefore its emptyDir volume, is untouched, so the first `cat` still prints 'v1'. Deleting the Pod is categorically different -- the Pod object is gone, and the kubelet cleans up the emptyDir directory it was backing on that node. The ReplicaSet's replacement Pod, `cache-pod-7f2ab`, is a new object built from the same template, but Kubernetes makes no attempt to carry forward the old Pod's emptyDir contents -- there's no mechanism that even could, since emptyDir has no identity independent of the specific Pod it was created for. The second `cat` therefore fails with 'No such file or directory'.

exercises.prompt: A single-replica Deployment runs a small key-value cache that's supposed to survive node maintenance without losing its data directory. It uses hostPath so the data 'lives on real disk.' After the node it was running on was cordoned and drained for an OS patch, the Pod rescheduled successfully onto a different node, but came up with a completely empty data directory. Find and fix the design bug (not just a YAML typo).
exercises.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: kv-cache
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: kv-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: kv-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: kv-cache
          image: kv-cache:2.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          hostPath:
            path: /var/lib/kv-cache-data
            type: DirectoryOrCreate
hints: hostPath data is real and durable, but scoped to exactly one thing -- what is that one thing, and did the Pod's reschedule cross that boundary?
A Deployment-managed Pod has no guaranteed relationship to any specific node across a reschedule -- what kind of storage abstraction is actually node-independent?
The fix isn't a typo in this YAML -- it's swapping hostPath for a storage mechanism that isn't tied to a specific node's local disk at all, which the next concept covers directly.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: kv-cache
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: kv-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: kv-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: kv-cache
          image: kv-cache:2.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: kv-cache-data
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is architectural, not syntactic: hostPath ties `/data` to whichever node's local disk the Pod happened to be running on at the time -- node maintenance forcing a reschedule onto a different node is exactly the scenario hostPath cannot survive, because the new node's `/var/lib/kv-cache-data` has never been written to. The real fix is to stop coupling the Pod's storage to a specific node at all, by requesting storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim instead (`claimName: kv-cache-data`, referencing a PVC backed by network-attached storage such as a cloud block volume). That storage exists as its own resource, independent of any node, and can be attached to whichever node the rescheduled Pod actually lands on -- exactly the property hostPath structurally cannot offer, and exactly what the PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims concept covers next.

assessments.prompt: A single-container Pod's container crashes and is restarted in place by the kubelet. Which of the following correctly describes what happens to an emptyDir volume mounted into that container?
options: The emptyDir volume's contents are wiped, because a new container instance always gets a fresh filesystem, including any mounted volumes.
The emptyDir volume's contents survive, because the volume is scoped to the Pod, not to the individual container instance running inside it.
The emptyDir volume's contents survive only if medium: Memory was set; otherwise they are wiped along with the container's writable layer.
Kubernetes automatically copies the emptyDir contents to a new location before restarting the container, then copies them back.
assessments.explanation: emptyDir is explicitly a Pod-scoped volume: the directory backing it lives on the node for as long as the Pod exists there, independent of any single container's lifecycle. A container restart replaces the container's own writable layer with a fresh one, but has no effect on the Pod-level emptyDir mount, which is exactly why it survives. Option A conflates the container's own ephemeral writable layer (which genuinely is wiped on restart) with the separate emptyDir volume. Option C inverts the actual distinction, which is about backing medium (disk vs tmpfs) affecting node-reboot survival, not container-restart survival. Option D describes a copy mechanism that doesn't exist -- nothing needs to be copied because the directory was never removed in the first place.

assessments.prompt: A container writes its own application logs to a local file at /var/log/app.log instead of stdout, with no volume mounted at that path. The container crashes and the kubelet restarts it in place. Can `kubectl logs --previous` retrieve the pre-crash contents of /var/log/app.log?
options: Yes -- kubectl logs --previous always retrieves the full filesystem state of the previous container instance, including any files it wrote to local disk.

No -- kubectl logs --previous only retrieves what the previous container instance wrote to stdout/stderr, which is entirely separate from its writable filesystem layer; a file written to local disk and never sent to stdout is already gone the moment that container instance exits, restart or not.
Yes, but only if the container's root filesystem was configured with medium: Memory.
No -- kubectl logs --previous only works for Pods that have already been deleted, not for a container restarted in place within a still-running Pod.
assessments.explanation: kubectl logs --previous surfaces the stdout/stderr stream the kubelet captured from the previous container instance -- it has nothing to do with that container's writable filesystem layer, which is an entirely separate thing and is discarded the instant the container exits, regardless of restart. A file written only to local disk and never emitted to stdout is unrecoverable through this command or any other, which is exactly why this concept calls out writing logs to stdout as the safer default. Option C invents a dependency on emptyDir's memory-backing option that has nothing to do with logs at all. Option D is wrong -- --previous works precisely for a container restarted in place within a still-running Pod; that's its primary use case.

assessments.prompt: A Pod's emptyDir volume is configured with `medium: Memory` instead of the default disk backing. Compared to a default, disk-backed emptyDir, what is the practical tradeoff?
options: It behaves identically in every respect -- medium: Memory is purely a performance hint with no functional difference in durability.

The memory-backed volume's usage counts against the Pod's memory limit, and its data is lost even faster than a disk-backed emptyDir -- including on a full Pod-level tmpfs remount, and certainly on a node reboot -- since it's never written to persistent disk at all.
It survives a node reboot, unlike a disk-backed emptyDir, because tmpfs contents are automatically checkpointed to disk before a controlled shutdown.
It automatically converts into a PersistentVolume once the amount of data written exceeds a configurable size threshold.
assessments.explanation: medium: Memory backs the emptyDir with tmpfs rather than the node's real disk, which is useful for latency-sensitive scratch data, but it comes with two real costs: that memory usage counts directly against the Pod's memory limit (unlike disk-backed emptyDir, which doesn't consume the Pod's memory budget), and the data is even more fragile than normal emptyDir, disappearing on events like a full remount and certainly never surviving a node reboot, since tmpfs by definition never touches persistent storage. Option A understates the real tradeoffs. Option C invents a checkpointing mechanism that doesn't exist. Option D invents an automatic-conversion behavior that has no basis in how emptyDir works.

assessments.prompt: Per this concept's own guidance, which scenario is hostPath actually a reasonable, appropriate design choice for, given that it permanently ties data to one specific node?
options: A ReplicaSet-managed web application caching rendered pages, since using hostPath will helpfully cause the scheduler to avoid ever moving those Pods to a different node.

A DaemonSet Pod that needs to read that specific node's own log directory or interact with that node's own Docker socket, since a DaemonSet is itself inherently node-scoped by design, matching hostPath's own scope exactly.
A StatefulSet running a clustered database, since a StatefulSet's ordinal identity guarantee ensures the replacement Pod always lands back on the exact same node.
Any workload at all, as long as replicas: 1 is set, since a single replica removes any possibility of a reschedule ever occurring.
assessments.explanation: This concept is explicit that hostPath is 'a node-scoped escape hatch, appropriate mainly for workloads that are themselves inherently node-scoped by design' -- a DaemonSet is exactly that kind of workload, since by definition it runs one Pod per node and genuinely wants that specific node's own local resources. Option A is false and backwards -- hostPath doesn't influence scheduling decisions at all; the scheduler remains completely free to move a ReplicaSet's Pods regardless of what volumes they mount. Option C is false -- a StatefulSet's ordinal identity guarantees a stable Pod name and, via volumeClaimTemplates, a stable PVC -- it says nothing about which node the Pod lands on, so hostPath under a StatefulSet has exactly the same node-mismatch risk as under a Deployment. Option D is false -- a single replica can still be rescheduled onto a different node after a node failure or drain, with the exact same data-loss consequence described in this concept.

assessments.prompt: Explain, precisely, the difference in scope between a container's writable filesystem layer, an emptyDir volume, and a hostPath volume, and why none of the three actually satisfies the general requirement 'this Pod's data must survive being rescheduled onto a different node.'
assessments.modelAnswer: Each of the three has a different, specific scope, and none of those scopes matches what a genuinely durable, reschedulable workload needs. A container's own writable filesystem layer is scoped to that one container instance -- when the kubelet restarts a crashed container in place, it starts a brand-new container with a brand-new, empty writable layer, so anything written only there is lost on every single restart, even within the same Pod. An emptyDir volume is scoped one level up, to the Pod as a whole: it survives a container restarting inside that Pod, since the Pod object and its emptyDir directory on the node are untouched by that event, but the moment the Pod itself is deleted, evicted, or replaced -- a coarser, Pod-level event -- the kubelet removes the emptyDir directory, and a replacement Pod (even from an identical template) starts with a fresh, empty one, with zero data carried forward. A hostPath volume is scoped to a specific node's real, persistent disk: it survives both a container restart and a Pod deletion, as long as the replacement Pod lands back on that exact same node -- but nothing about how a ReplicaSet or Deployment schedules replacement Pods guarantees that at all; the scheduler is free to place the new Pod on any node with sufficient resources, and if it picks a different one, the hostPath now refers to an entirely different, empty directory there. The common requirement missing from all three is storage that is durable across Pod replacement AND independent of which specific node the replacement happens to land on -- decoupled from any one node's local disk entirely, so it can be attached to a Pod wherever the scheduler puts it. That's precisely the gap PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims are built to close, by representing storage as its own cluster resource rather than as something anchored to a Pod's or a node's own local lifecycle.

concepts.title: PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims
concepts.description: Kubernetes splits storage into two separate objects on purpose -- a PersistentVolumeClaim describing what a Pod needs in the abstract, and a PersistentVolume representing what storage actually is underneath -- so that a Pod spec never has to know or care whether its data lives on an AWS EBS volume, a GCE disk, or an NFS share.
learningObjectives: Explain the specific abstraction PersistentVolumeClaims and PersistentVolumes split apart: what a Pod asks for versus what storage actually is.
Distinguish a PersistentVolume (a cluster-scoped resource representing real storage) from a PersistentVolumeClaim (a namespaced request that binds to one).
Explain what a StorageClass and its provisioner do, and how dynamic provisioning removes the need to hand-create PersistentVolumes.
Explain access modes (ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany), and correct the common misunderstanding of what ReadWriteOnce actually restricts.
Predict what happens to the underlying storage when a PVC is deleted, based on reclaim policy.
Trace the binding lifecycle from a PVC's creation to a Pod actually mounting the resulting storage.

sections.heading: Splitting 'What a Pod Needs' From 'What Storage Actually Is'
sections.body:
A Pod spec that references a `hostPath` directly is coupled, in one single YAML file, to a very specific fact about the physical world -- 'the data lives at this exact path on this exact node.' PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims exist specifically to break that coupling into two independent halves.

A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is what a Pod's author actually writes: a request expressed entirely in the abstract -- 'I need 10Gi of storage, mountable read-write by a single node, ideally on fast SSD-backed storage' -- with zero mention of any specific disk, cloud provider, or node. A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is the other half: an object representing one specific, real chunk of storage -- an AWS EBS volume, a GCE Persistent Disk, an NFS export, a Ceph RBD image -- along with its actual capacity and supported access modes. Crucially, a PV is a **cluster-scoped** resource (no namespace), because the physical storage it represents doesn't inherently belong to any one team's namespace, while a PVC is **namespaced**, because it's the application-facing request that lives alongside the Pods that will use it.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: db-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  containers:
    - name: postgres
      image: postgres:16
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: db-data
```

The Pod spec above says only `claimName: db-data` -- it never names a cloud provider, a disk type, or a size directly. Swap the underlying PV from an EBS-backed one to an NFS-backed one, in a completely different cluster, and this exact Pod spec doesn't change at all.

sections.heading: Static vs. Dynamic Provisioning, and StorageClasses
sections.body:
In the earliest, simplest model -- **static provisioning** -- a cluster administrator hand-creates a batch of PersistentVolume objects ahead of time, each describing a real disk that already exists, and PVCs bind to whichever pre-created PV happens to match their requested size and access mode closely enough. This works, but it requires a human to anticipate demand and provision real storage in advance, which doesn't scale well and reintroduces exactly the kind of manual toil Kubernetes is generally trying to eliminate.

**Dynamic provisioning** removes that human from the loop entirely. A **StorageClass** names a **provisioner** -- a plugin that knows how to talk to a specific storage backend's API (create an EBS volume of a given size, create a GCE Persistent Disk, and so on) -- plus backend-specific parameters (disk type, IOPS, filesystem type):

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
```

When a PVC names this StorageClass (`storageClassName: fast-ssd`), the provisioner is invoked automatically, on demand, the moment the PVC needs to bind -- it calls out to the cloud provider's API, creates a brand-new real disk of the requested size, and creates the matching PV object to represent it, with no administrator involved for that specific request at all. A PVC that omits `storageClassName` entirely uses whichever StorageClass the cluster has marked as its default (via an annotation); a PVC that explicitly sets `storageClassName: ""` deliberately opts out of dynamic provisioning altogether and will only ever bind to a pre-existing, statically-provisioned PV.

sections.heading: Binding: How a Claim Actually Finds Its Volume
sections.body:
A separate binding controller continuously watches for PVCs that aren't yet bound and PVs that are available, and tries to match them -- comparing requested capacity (a PV must have at least as much as requested, though it's typically an exact or near-exact match with dynamic provisioning), access modes, `storageClassName`, and any label selector the PVC specifies. Binding is strictly one-to-one: once a PV is bound to a PVC, it's exclusively reserved for that PVC and won't be offered to any other claim, even if it technically has excess capacity.

With dynamic provisioning, this whole sequence usually completes in seconds and is easy to miss happening at all -- but it's worth watching once, because `Pending` is a state you will eventually have to debug:

```bash
kubectl get pvc db-data
# NAME      STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES
# db-data   Pending                                        <-- provisioning in progress

# a few seconds later...
kubectl get pvc db-data
# NAME      STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES
# db-data   Bound    pvc-3f8a1c2e-...                           10Gi       RWO
```

A PVC stuck in `Pending` indefinitely almost always means one of: no StorageClass exists matching the name it requested (a typo is extremely common), no default StorageClass is configured and the PVC didn't name one, or the requested access mode isn't something any available PV or provisioner can satisfy -- `kubectl describe pvc` surfaces the specific reason as an event, and is the first thing to check, exactly the same debugging instinct as checking `kubectl get endpoints` first for a Service with no traffic.

sections.heading: Access Modes: What ReadWriteOnce Actually Restricts
sections.body:
The three access modes are **ReadWriteOnce (RWO)** -- mountable read-write by a single node; **ReadOnlyMany (ROX)** -- mountable read-only by many nodes simultaneously; and **ReadWriteMany (RWX)** -- mountable read-write by many nodes simultaneously.

The single most common misreading is assuming ReadWriteOnce means 'only one Pod.' It doesn't -- it means one **node**. Several Pods scheduled onto the *same* node can all mount and write to the same RWO-backed volume concurrently without any conflict at the Kubernetes level; RWO only prevents that same volume from being simultaneously mounted read-write on a *second, different* node. This is exactly why most raw block storage (AWS EBS, GCE Persistent Disks, Azure Disks) only supports RWO in the first place: the underlying block-device attachment mechanism is fundamentally a single-node concept -- a block device gets attached to one machine's kernel at a time, full stop, regardless of how many processes or containers on that machine subsequently open it.

Getting genuine ReadWriteMany support requires a backend that's a real network filesystem from the ground up, not a block device pretending to be one -- NFS, CephFS, Amazon EFS, Azure Files. This is also precisely why requesting `accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]` against a StorageClass whose provisioner only creates EBS volumes results in a PVC stuck permanently `Pending`: the provisioner is perfectly capable of creating the disk, but it can never create one that satisfies an access mode its underlying technology structurally cannot support.

sections.heading: Reclaim Policy: What Happens When the Claim Is Deleted
sections.body:
`persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy` governs what happens to a PV -- and the real storage it represents -- once its bound PVC is deleted. **Delete** removes the PV object and instructs the provisioner to actually delete the underlying real storage (the actual EBS volume, the actual disk) -- this is the default `reclaimPolicy` for most dynamically-provisioned StorageClasses, and it means deleting a PVC is a genuinely irreversible, destructive action, not routine cleanup. **Retain** keeps both the PV object (now in a `Released` state, no longer bindable to a new PVC without manual intervention) and the underlying data fully intact, requiring an administrator to explicitly decide what to do with it -- reattach it to a new PVC by hand, or delete it deliberately.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pvc-3f8a1c2e
spec:
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  csi:
    driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: vol-0abcd1234
```

The practical implication is worth stating plainly: if a database's PVC uses a StorageClass with `reclaimPolicy: Delete` (the common default), a `kubectl delete pvc` -- whether deliberate, accidental, or the side effect of deleting an owning object that cascades down to it -- can permanently destroy the actual data with no recovery path at all. This is exactly why teams running anything genuinely important either override the StorageClass's reclaim policy to `Retain` for that workload, maintain independent backups outside the PV/PVC mechanism entirely, or -- as covered in the next concept -- rely on a StatefulSet's own safeguards around per-replica storage, which still doesn't make `Delete` any less destructive on its own.

examples.title: The Full Path From PVC to Pod, With Dynamic Provisioning
examples.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: standard
provisioner: kubernetes.io/aws-ebs
parameters:
  type: gp3
reclaimPolicy: Delete
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: db-data
spec:
  storageClassName: standard
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
examples.explanation: Applying just these two objects -- no PersistentVolume anywhere in this file -- is enough to end up with a fully bound, usable 20Gi volume. The moment `db-data` is created, the binding controller sees it's unbound and references the `standard` StorageClass, which triggers that StorageClass's provisioner (`kubernetes.io/aws-ebs`) to create a real 20Gi gp3 EBS volume behind the scenes and generate a matching PersistentVolume object for it automatically. `kubectl get pv` would show a PV with an auto-generated name like `pvc-<uuid>` appearing shortly after the PVC, already bound to `db-data` -- nobody wrote that PV object by hand at any point.

examples.title: A PVC Stuck Pending Due to an Unsatisfiable Access Mode
examples.code:
kubectl get pvc shared-cache
# NAME           STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
# shared-cache   Pending                                     ebs-gp3

kubectl describe pvc shared-cache
# ...
# Events:
#   Type     Reason              Message
#   ----     ------              -------
#   Warning  ProvisioningFailed  failed to provision volume: rpc error: invalid parameter: access mode ReadWriteMany not supported by driver ebs.csi.aws.com
examples.explanation: The PVC requested `ReadWriteMany`, but the `ebs-gp3` StorageClass's provisioner creates AWS EBS volumes, and EBS is block storage that fundamentally supports only single-node attachment -- there is no way for this specific provisioner to ever satisfy a ReadWriteMany request, no matter how long it's left Pending. `kubectl describe pvc` surfaces exactly this reason as an event, which is the fastest way to distinguish 'this will resolve itself in a few more seconds' from 'this is structurally impossible and needs a different StorageClass entirely' (one backed by EFS or another genuine network filesystem, in this case).

misconceptions.description: ReadWriteOnce means only one Pod can mount the volume for writing at a time -- if two Pods both try to use it, one will be blocked.
misconceptions.clarification: ReadWriteOnce restricts mounting to a single node, not a single Pod. Multiple Pods scheduled onto that same node can all mount and write to the same RWO volume concurrently with no conflict from Kubernetes' side (whether that's actually safe depends on the application and filesystem, not on the access mode). What RWO actually prevents is a second Pod on a *different* node from also mounting it read-write, which is a constraint of the underlying block-storage attachment mechanism, not an arbitrary Kubernetes-imposed limit.

misconceptions.description: A PersistentVolumeClaim is a lightweight, harmless pointer to a PersistentVolume -- deleting one is routine cleanup, not something to think twice about.
misconceptions.clarification: Whether deleting a PVC is harmless depends entirely on its reclaim policy. With the common `Delete` reclaim policy (the default for many dynamically-provisioned StorageClasses), deleting the PVC triggers actual deletion of the real underlying storage -- the cloud disk itself -- which is an irreversible loss of whatever data was on it, not a no-op. Only under `Retain` does deleting the PVC leave the underlying PV and its data intact for manual recovery.

exercises.prompt: A cluster has exactly one StorageClass, `ebs-gp3`, whose provisioner only supports ReadWriteOnce. Someone applies a PVC requesting `accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]` against that StorageClass, intending to share one volume across Pods on several different nodes. What state will the PVC end up in, and will it ever change on its own?
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: shared-uploads
spec:
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
hints: Does the provisioner for ebs-gp3 have any way at all to create a volume that multiple nodes can mount read-write simultaneously?
Compare a Pending PVC that's waiting on a slow-but-working provisioning call versus one requesting something the provisioner can never technically deliver.
Check what kubectl describe pvc would report as the event reason here.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It stays Pending indefinitely -- it will not resolve on its own, no matter how long you wait. EBS-backed storage is fundamentally block storage that only supports single-node attachment, so the ebs-gp3 provisioner has no way to ever satisfy a ReadWriteMany request; this isn't a slow provisioning operation, it's a structurally unsatisfiable one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Unlike a normal provisioning delay (typically resolved within seconds), this PVC requests an access mode that the only available StorageClass's underlying technology cannot provide under any circumstances -- AWS EBS volumes attach to exactly one node at a time, by design, at the infrastructure level, regardless of what Kubernetes asks for. The binding/provisioning controller will keep trying and keep failing, surfacing a ProvisioningFailed event via kubectl describe pvc, but there is no amount of waiting that fixes this -- the actual fix requires either changing the access mode to ReadWriteOnce (if single-node access is actually sufficient) or provisioning against a genuinely different StorageClass backed by a real network filesystem (NFS, EFS, CephFS) that can honor ReadWriteMany.

exercises.prompt: A team's PVC has been Pending for twenty minutes. They insist the StorageClass name is correct because 'fast-ssd' is what their platform team told them to use. Find the actual bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: db-data
spec:
  storageClassName: Fast-SSD
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
hints: StorageClass names, like most Kubernetes object names, are matched as exact strings -- run kubectl get storageclass and compare character by character, including case.
Kubernetes resource names are conventionally all-lowercase, and StorageClass name matching does not normalize case for you.
The fix is a one-character-case change in the PVC, not anything on the StorageClass object itself.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: db-data
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
exercises.solutionExplanation: The PVC references `Fast-SSD`, but the actual StorageClass object is named `fast-ssd` (lowercase) -- `kubectl get storageclass` would show the real name plainly. StorageClass name references are exact-string matches with no case normalization, exactly like Service label selectors, so `Fast-SSD` simply doesn't refer to anything that exists, and the PVC can never bind or provision against a StorageClass that isn't there. Correcting the case to match the real object name (`fast-ssd`) lets the provisioner pick up the PVC normally, and it should move to Bound within seconds.

assessments.prompt: What does an access mode of ReadWriteOnce (RWO) actually restrict?
options: Only one Pod, cluster-wide, may ever mount the volume, even read-only Pods on the same node as the writer.
Only one node may mount the volume read-write at a time; multiple Pods co-located on that same node can all mount and write to it concurrently.
Only one namespace may contain PVCs that reference the underlying PersistentVolume.
The volume may only be written to once, after which it becomes permanently read-only.
assessments.explanation: ReadWriteOnce is a node-level restriction, not a Pod-level one -- it reflects the fact that the underlying technology (typically a block device) can only be attached to a single node's kernel at a time. Any number of Pods scheduled onto that one node can mount and write to it simultaneously without conflict. Option A overstates the restriction to the Pod level, which is the single most common misreading of RWO. Option C confuses access mode with namespace scoping, an unrelated concept. Option D describes something closer to a write-once medium, which isn't what RWO means at all -- RWO volumes can be written to repeatedly for as long as they're mounted read-write.

assessments.prompt: Why is a PersistentVolume a cluster-scoped resource (no namespace), while a PersistentVolumeClaim is namespaced?
options: It's an arbitrary API design choice with no underlying reason -- either object could have been namespaced or cluster-scoped with no practical difference.

The real, physical storage a PV represents doesn't inherently belong to any one team's namespace, while a PVC is the application-facing request that naturally lives alongside the specific Pods and namespace that will actually consume it.
PersistentVolumes are actually namespaced too, but only become visible to users holding cluster-admin RBAC permissions.
A PersistentVolume must be cluster-scoped because only cluster-scoped objects are permitted to trigger a StorageClass's provisioner.
assessments.explanation: This split mirrors the deliberate abstraction the whole PV/PVC system is built around: the PV represents a real, physical resource that exists independently of any particular application team, so scoping it to a namespace wouldn't reflect reality -- a disk isn't 'owned' by a namespace the way an application's own objects are. The PVC, by contrast, is specifically the application-facing request, so it lives in the namespace of the Pods that will use it, exactly like other namespaced objects such as Deployments and Services. Option A dismisses a design choice that has a clear rationale. Option C is factually wrong -- PVs are genuinely cluster-scoped, not namespace-scoped-but-hidden. Option D invents a nonexistent admission rule.

assessments.prompt: What is the actual difference between a PVC that omits `storageClassName` entirely and one that explicitly sets `storageClassName: ""`?
options: There is no difference at all -- both are treated identically by the binding controller.

Omitting the field causes the PVC to use whichever StorageClass the cluster has marked as default; explicitly setting it to an empty string deliberately opts out of dynamic provisioning altogether, so the PVC will only ever bind to a pre-existing, statically-provisioned PV.
Omitting the field opts out of dynamic provisioning entirely, while explicitly setting an empty string requests whichever StorageClass currently has the fastest provisioner.
Both settings leave the PVC permanently unbound unless a StorageClass is added to the cluster afterward.
assessments.explanation: This is a real, meaningful distinction called out directly in this concept: leaving storageClassName unset lets the cluster's default StorageClass (marked via an annotation) apply automatically, while explicitly setting it to an empty string is a deliberate signal that this PVC should never be dynamically provisioned, and should only bind to a PV that already exists from static provisioning. Option A collapses a distinction that genuinely changes behavior. Option C reverses the actual behavior of the two settings. Option D is wrong for the omitted-field case, which resolves to the default StorageClass rather than staying unbound.

assessments.prompt: A PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy is set to Retain. Its bound PVC is deleted. What state does the PV enter, and can a brand-new PVC automatically bind to it afterward?
options: The PV is deleted immediately along with the PVC, exactly as it would be under a Delete reclaim policy -- Retain only protects the underlying cloud disk, not the PV object itself.
The PV enters a Released state, with its underlying data left fully intact, but it cannot be automatically bound to a new PVC -- an administrator must explicitly intervene first.
The PV immediately reverts to Available and silently rebinds to the very next PVC that requests a matching capacity and access mode, with no administrator action needed.
The PV keeps its original Bound status indefinitely, even with no PVC referencing it, until the entire cluster is restarted.
assessments.explanation: Retain's entire purpose is to prevent automatic destruction or automatic reuse: when the bound PVC is deleted, the PV object and its underlying real storage both survive fully intact, but the PV moves to Released rather than back to Available, specifically so it can't be silently claimed by an unrelated PVC that happens to request a similar size and access mode -- a human has to look at it and deliberately decide what to do next. Option A describes Delete's behavior, the opposite of what Retain does to the PV object. Option C describes the kind of automatic rebinding Retain specifically prevents. Option D invents a restart dependency that doesn't reflect how the state transition actually works.

assessments.prompt: Walk through, layer by layer, what happens when a Pod referencing a PersistentVolumeClaim is created in a cluster using dynamic provisioning -- from the PVC itself down to the real disk -- and explain specifically what a reclaim policy governs in that chain.
assessments.modelAnswer: When the PVC is first created, it's simply a namespaced object recording an abstract request -- a capacity, a set of access modes, and optionally a StorageClass name -- with no PersistentVolume bound to it yet, so it starts in a Pending state. The binding/provisioning machinery notices the unbound PVC and reads its `storageClassName` (or the cluster's default StorageClass if none was set), which names a specific provisioner plugin responsible for a particular storage backend. That provisioner is invoked with the PVC's requested capacity and parameters, and it calls out to the actual backend's API -- for example, the AWS EBS CSI driver calling AWS's own API to create a brand-new EBS volume of the requested size -- and once that real disk exists, the provisioner creates a matching PersistentVolume object in the cluster representing it, and the binding controller marks the PVC as Bound to that specific PV, one-to-one. Only once the PVC is Bound can a Pod referencing it (via `volumes: - persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: ...`) actually be scheduled with that volume attached and mounted -- the kubelet on whichever node the Pod lands on is responsible for the actual attach-and-mount operation using the storage driver, at which point the container sees an ordinary mounted filesystem at whatever path it specified. The reclaim policy governs specifically what happens at the *other* end of this chain, when the PVC is later deleted: with `Delete`, the provisioner is instructed to actually tear down the real disk it created (deleting the EBS volume itself, not just the Kubernetes objects representing it), making PVC deletion a genuinely destructive, irreversible action; with `Retain`, the real disk and its data are left completely intact, and the PV transitions to a Released state, requiring a human to explicitly decide to reuse or delete it -- the reclaim policy has no effect at all on the create/bind/mount side of the chain, only on what happens to the underlying storage once its claim goes away.

concepts.title: StatefulSets: Stable Identity for Stateful Workloads
concepts.description: A Deployment treats every Pod as a disposable, interchangeable copy of the same template -- exactly right for a stateless web tier, and exactly wrong for a clustered database where each replica needs a stable name, its own dedicated storage, and a predictable startup order; StatefulSet is the controller built specifically to provide all three.
learningObjectives: Explain why a Deployment's interchangeable, randomly-named Pods are a poor fit for a clustered, stateful workload like a database.
Describe the three specific guarantees a StatefulSet provides: ordinal Pod identity, stable per-replica storage via volumeClaimTemplates, and ordered Pod creation/scaling/deletion.
Explain how StatefulSet Pod naming (ordinal suffixes) differs from a ReplicaSet's hash-based naming, and why a replaced Pod keeps the same name.
Explain how volumeClaimTemplates produce one PVC per replica that reattaches to the same ordinal across Pod replacement, unlike a Deployment's Pod-level volumes.
Explain the role of a headless Service in giving each StatefulSet Pod its own individually addressable identity.
Predict the order of Pod creation and termination during a StatefulSet's scale-up, scale-down, and rolling update.

sections.heading: Why a Deployment Doesn't Fit a Clustered Database
sections.body:
Recall from the Deployments concept that a ReplicaSet's Pods are, deliberately, fully interchangeable: any one of three replicas can be deleted and replaced by an equivalent Pod with a new random name and a new IP, and nothing about the system's correctness depends on which specific Pod is running -- that's precisely what makes a stateless web tier trivially scalable and self-healing.

A clustered, stateful workload -- a Postgres primary with read replicas, a Kafka broker cluster, a Cassandra or Elasticsearch ring -- breaks that assumption in a fundamental way. These replicas are **not** interchangeable: each one typically has a distinct role or a distinct slice of data (the primary versus a replica, broker 0 versus broker 2, the node currently holding a particular data shard), needs to be reliably reachable at a *specific, predictable* address by its peers (not 'any one of the pool,' but 'specifically the primary' or 'specifically broker 2'), and needs its *own* durable slice of storage that follows it specifically across restarts, not a fresh volume drawn from a shared, undifferentiated pool. A ReplicaSet has no concept of any of this -- it manages a count of identical things, full stop -- which is exactly the gap StatefulSet is designed to close.

sections.heading: Stable, Predictable Identity: Ordinal Pod Names
sections.body:
A StatefulSet names its Pods `<statefulset-name>-<ordinal>` -- `web-0`, `web-1`, `web-2` -- rather than the random hash suffix a ReplicaSet generates. This is a small-looking detail with a large consequence: the name is not just predictable, it's **stable across replacement**. If `web-1` is deleted for any reason, the StatefulSet controller creates a replacement Pod that is again named `web-1` -- the exact same ordinal, not a new random identity -- unlike a Deployment, where a replaced Pod always gets a brand-new generated name with no relationship to the one it replaced.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  serviceName: web
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: my-db:1.0
```

By default (the `OrderedReady` pod management policy), Pods are also created strictly in ascending ordinal order on scale-up -- `web-0` must be Running and Ready before `web-1` is even created, and so on -- and deleted in strictly descending ordinal order on scale-down or deletion -- the highest-numbered Pod goes first. This predictability matters for real reasons, not just tidiness: a quorum-based system bootstrapping its first member, or a scale-down that should shed the most recently added replica rather than an arbitrary one, both depend on this exact ordering.

sections.heading: Stable Storage Per Replica: volumeClaimTemplates
sections.body:
A StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplates` field describes a PVC template that gets stamped out **once per ordinal**, not once for the whole StatefulSet -- `web-0` gets its own PVC (conventionally named `<template-name>-web-0`), `web-1` gets its own separate PVC (`<template-name>-web-1`), and so on.

```yaml
spec:
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
```

The crucial guarantee: when `web-1` specifically is deleted and replaced, the replacement Pod -- again named `web-1` -- is reattached to that **same** PVC (`data-web-1`), and therefore the same underlying PV and the same actual data, rather than getting a fresh, empty volume. This is the mechanism that actually makes 'replica 1's data survives replica 1 being rescheduled' true in practice, and it has no equivalent at all in a plain Deployment: a Deployment's Pod template can reference at most one shared PVC name for every replica, which either means every replica would fight over exclusive access to the same single volume (impossible for RWO storage across different nodes, and actively dangerous even on the same node without careful application-level coordination) or, more commonly, that Deployments simply aren't used with per-replica durable storage at all -- volumeClaimTemplates exist specifically because a Deployment structurally cannot express 'each replica gets its own dedicated, identity-linked volume.'

sections.heading: Headless Services and Per-Pod DNS Identity
sections.body:
A StatefulSet is normally paired with a **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`), named via the StatefulSet's own `serviceName` field. As covered in the Services concept, a headless Service has no virtual IP for kube-proxy to rewrite toward -- instead, DNS lookups against it return the individual IPs of every currently-Ready backing Pod directly.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 5432
```

When this headless Service governs a StatefulSet, each Pod additionally receives its **own** individual DNS record of the form `<pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` -- for example, `web-1.web.default.svc.cluster.local` -- resolving specifically and only to that one Pod's own IP. This is precisely the mechanism that lets a peer in a clustered database address 'specifically replica 1' rather than 'whichever replica happens to answer,' which is exactly the requirement an ordinary, load-balancing ClusterIP Service cannot satisfy -- it would only ever hand back one shared virtual IP with no way to target an individual, specific member behind it.

sections.heading: Ordered Scaling and Rolling Updates
sections.body:
Scaling a StatefulSet up from 1 to 3 creates `web-1` only after `web-0` is Running and Ready, then `web-2` only after `web-1` is Running and Ready -- strictly sequential, by default. Scaling down from 3 to 1 reverses this exactly: `web-2` is deleted first, then `web-1`, leaving `web-0` -- the highest ordinals go first, never an arbitrary one, and never in parallel.

Worth flagging as an edge case: scaling down does **not**, by default, delete the PVCs belonging to the removed ordinals (`data-web-1`, `data-web-2` stick around, retaining their data) -- scaling back up to 3 later reattaches `web-1` and `web-2` to those very same PVCs, picking up right where they left off, rather than starting fresh. (Newer Kubernetes versions expose this behavior explicitly via `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`, letting you opt into deleting per-replica PVCs on scale-down instead, if that's actually what a given workload wants.)

Rolling updates follow the same descending-ordinal discipline: the highest-numbered Pod is updated (deleted and recreated with the new template) first, and the controller waits for it to become Ready before moving to the next-highest ordinal -- the reverse of the ascending-ordinal order used for initial scale-up. A `Parallel` pod management policy exists as an explicit opt-out of all this ordering, for StatefulSet users who only want the identity and storage guarantees without paying the sequential-startup cost -- worth knowing it exists, precisely because it demonstrates that the ordering and the identity/storage guarantees are genuinely separable properties, not one indivisible package.

examples.title: A StatefulSet With Per-Replica Storage and a Headless Service
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  serviceName: web
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
examples.explanation: Applying this produces `web-0`, `web-1`, `web-2` in that strict order, each with its own PVC (`data-web-0`, `data-web-1`, `data-web-2`) and its own individual DNS name (`web-0.web...`, `web-1.web...`, `web-2.web...`). Note that `serviceName: web` on the StatefulSet is what links it to the headless Service of the same name -- that's the field that actually causes the per-Pod DNS records to be created; a StatefulSet with no matching headless Service still gets stable Pod names and per-replica storage, but not the individual DNS entries.

examples.title: A Replaced Pod Keeps Its Name and Reattaches to Its Own PVC
examples.code:
kubectl get pods -l app=web
# web-0   Running
# web-1   Running
# web-2   Running

kubectl delete pod web-1

kubectl get pods -l app=web
# web-0   Running
# web-1   Running   <-- same name, new Pod object
# web-2   Running

kubectl get pod web-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes[0].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName}'
# data-web-1   <-- reattached to the SAME PVC it always had
examples.explanation: The replacement Pod is again named `web-1` -- the StatefulSet controller specifically recreates whichever ordinal was removed, rather than assigning a new one -- and it mounts the exact same PVC, `data-web-1`, that the previous `web-1` used, so whatever data was written before the deletion is still there after the replacement comes up. Contrast this directly with a Deployment-managed Pod deletion, where the replacement gets an entirely new generated name and, absent volumeClaimTemplates (which Deployments don't support at all), no durable per-replica storage concept to reattach to in the first place.

misconceptions.description: A StatefulSet is basically a slower Deployment -- Pods just come up one at a time instead of all together, and otherwise they're interchangeable.
misconceptions.clarification: The sequential creation is a side effect of what a StatefulSet actually guarantees, not the point of it. The real distinguishing features are stable, replacement-surviving Pod identity (the same ordinal name every time) and stable, replacement-surviving per-replica storage (volumeClaimTemplates reattaching the same PVC to the same ordinal) -- properties a Deployment has no mechanism to provide at all, regardless of how you configure its rollout pace. Swapping a StatefulSet for a Deployment 'just to go faster' would silently drop both of those guarantees, not merely change the timing.

misconceptions.description: Deleting a StatefulSet-managed Pod (say, web-1) causes Kubernetes to create a brand-new, differently-identified replacement, the same way deleting a Deployment-managed Pod does.
misconceptions.clarification: A StatefulSet's controller specifically recreates the same ordinal that was deleted -- the replacement is again named web-1, not some new generated name -- and reattaches it to the same PVC that ordinal has always owned, carrying its data forward. This is the opposite of a Deployment-managed Pod's replacement, which gets a fresh random name and, without volumeClaimTemplates (a StatefulSet-only feature), no durable per-replica storage identity to preserve in the first place.

exercises.prompt: A StatefulSet named cache has 3 replicas (cache-0, cache-1, cache-2) with volumeClaimTemplates. It's scaled down to 1, then back up to 3. In what order are Pods deleted during the scale-down, in what order are they recreated during the scale-up, and do cache-1 and cache-2 come back with fresh, empty volumes or their previous data?
exercises.code:
kubectl scale statefulset cache --replicas=1
# deletion order: ?

kubectl scale statefulset cache --replicas=3
# creation order: ?
# cache-1 and cache-2's volumes: fresh, or previous data?
hints: Scale-down removes the highest ordinals first, never an arbitrary one and never in parallel by default.
Scale-up recreates Pods in ascending order, waiting for each to become Ready before starting the next.
By default, does scaling a StatefulSet down actually delete the PVCs belonging to the removed ordinals, or only the Pods?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Scale-down deletes cache-2 first, then cache-1, leaving cache-0. Scale-up recreates cache-1 first, then cache-2, each waited on to become Ready before the next starts. Their volumes come back with their PREVIOUS data intact -- by default, scaling down does not delete the PVCs for the removed ordinals, so scaling back up reattaches cache-1 and cache-2 to the same data-cache-1 and data-cache-2 PVCs they had before.
exercises.solutionExplanation: StatefulSet scale-down always proceeds in strictly descending ordinal order -- the highest-numbered Pod is removed first -- so cache-2 goes before cache-1, leaving cache-0 as the sole survivor. Scaling back up to 3 proceeds in strictly ascending order, and under the default OrderedReady policy, cache-1 must be Running and Ready before cache-2 is even created. Critically, the PVCs created by volumeClaimTemplates for the now-removed ordinals are not deleted by a scale-down by default -- they're simply left bound but unused, still holding their data -- so when cache-1 and cache-2 are recreated on scale-up, the StatefulSet controller reattaches each to its own pre-existing PVC (data-cache-1, data-cache-2 respectively), and both come back with exactly the data they had before, not a fresh empty volume.

exercises.prompt: A team ran a 3-replica clustered cache as a Deployment, with a single PersistentVolumeClaim (ReadWriteOnce) referenced directly in the Pod template, expecting each replica to end up with its own independent slice of data. Instead, at most one Pod ever reaches Running (the other two stay Pending, 'volume node affinity conflict'), and when a single replica does run, all replicas that do come up appear to read and write the exact same shared data. Find and fix the underlying design bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: cache-node:1.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: cache-data
hints: A Deployment's Pod template can only name one single, specific PVC by name -- how many distinct volumes does that give you across 3 replicas?
ReadWriteOnce storage can only be mounted read-write on one node at a time -- what happens when replicas land on different nodes but all reference that same RWO claim?
This calls for per-replica storage, generated automatically once per ordinal -- which controller type actually provides that, and how?
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  serviceName: cache
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: cache-node:1.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original Deployment gives every one of its 3 replicas the exact same, single claimName: cache-data -- there is only ever one PVC involved, no matter how many replicas exist, because a Deployment's Pod template has no concept of a per-replica claim. Since that PVC is ReadWriteOnce, it can only be mounted read-write on one node at a time; any replica scheduled to a different node than whichever one already has it attached gets stuck Pending with a volume node affinity conflict, and any replicas that do happen to share a node are all reading and writing the identical shared volume, not independent data. Converting to a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates fixes this at the root: Kubernetes now generates one distinct PVC per ordinal (data-cache-0, data-cache-1, data-cache-2), so each replica gets its own dedicated 5Gi volume, can be scheduled to any node without conflicting with the others, and keeps that same specific volume across any future replacement of that ordinal.

assessments.prompt: A StatefulSet-managed Pod, web-2, is deleted (e.g. the node it was on failed). What is preserved for its replacement, compared to what a Deployment would preserve if it lost a Pod the same way?
options: Nothing meaningful is preserved in either case -- both controllers simply create a fresh Pod with no relationship to the one that was lost.

A StatefulSet's replacement keeps the same ordinal name (web-2 again) and reattaches to the same per-replica PVC; a Deployment's replacement gets an entirely new generated name and no equivalent per-replica storage concept at all.
Both controllers preserve the exact same Pod IP address for the replacement, since IPs are tied to ordinal/replica position in both cases.
A Deployment actually preserves more state than a StatefulSet, because ReplicaSets retain old Pod objects for rollback purposes.
assessments.explanation: This is the core practical difference: a StatefulSet's controller recreates the same ordinal (web-2) and, if volumeClaimTemplates are defined, reattaches that ordinal's own dedicated PVC, carrying its data forward. A Deployment has neither mechanism -- its ReplicaSet generates a fresh, randomly-suffixed name for any replacement Pod, and a Deployment's Pod template supports at most one shared PVC reference across all replicas, not a distinct one per replica. Option A ignores the entire point of StatefulSet's identity guarantees. Option C is false -- Pod IPs are never guaranteed stable across a replacement in either controller; only the StatefulSet's Pod *name* and per-ordinal storage are preserved, not its IP. Option D confuses ReplicaSet revision retention (for Deployment rollbacks) with per-Pod state preservation, which is an unrelated mechanism.

assessments.prompt: A team wants a StatefulSet's stable identity and per-replica storage guarantees, but doesn't want to pay the cost of strictly sequential Pod startup on scale-up. Which setting lets them opt out of the ordering specifically, without losing the other guarantees?
options: There is no such option -- ordered startup is an inseparable part of what makes something a StatefulSet at all; opting out requires switching to a Deployment and losing every other guarantee too.

Setting the Pod management policy to Parallel, which removes the strict ascending/descending creation-and-deletion ordering while leaving ordinal naming and volumeClaimTemplates-based per-replica storage completely intact.
Temporarily setting replicas to a negative number, which forces the controller to create every Pod simultaneously as a side effect.
Removing the serviceName field, since that field is what actually causes ordered startup, independent of any podManagementPolicy setting.
assessments.explanation: This concept explicitly calls out Parallel pod management policy as 'an explicit opt-out of all this ordering, for StatefulSet users who only want the identity and storage guarantees without paying the sequential-startup cost' -- proof that ordering and identity/storage are genuinely separable properties, not one indivisible package. Option A overstates ordering as inseparable from StatefulSet-ness, which Parallel itself disproves. Option C describes an invalid, nonsensical operation. Option D misattributes ordering to serviceName, which actually controls the headless Service link for per-Pod DNS, not Pod creation/deletion ordering.

assessments.prompt: A StatefulSet is deployed with correct volumeClaimTemplates and ordinal Pod naming, but its `serviceName` field points to a Service that doesn't exist yet, or that isn't actually headless. What specifically is lost as a result?
options: Nothing about ordinal Pod naming or per-replica storage is affected -- those operate independently of any Service; what's lost is specifically the individual per-Pod DNS records (like web-1.web...svc.cluster.local) that a correctly configured headless Service would otherwise provide.
The entire StatefulSet fails to create any Pods at all, since a valid, existing headless serviceName is a hard prerequisite the API server validates at admission time.
The Pods lose their ordinal names and revert to ReplicaSet-style random name suffixes.
Every replica's PVC is deleted immediately, since serviceName is a required input to persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.
assessments.explanation: The concept states this directly: 'a StatefulSet with no matching headless Service still gets stable Pod names and per-replica storage, but not the individual DNS entries.' Ordinal naming comes from the StatefulSet controller itself, and volumeClaimTemplates-based storage is independent of any Service; the only thing that genuinely depends on a correctly wired serviceName is the per-Pod DNS record used to address one specific replica by name. Options B, C, and D each invent a hard dependency that doesn't actually exist between serviceName and Pod creation, naming, or storage.

assessments.prompt: During a StatefulSet's initial scale-up, Pods are created in ascending ordinal order (0, then 1, then 2). During a rolling update to a new Pod template on an already-running StatefulSet, in what order are the existing Pods updated?
options: The same ascending order as scale-up -- 0 first, then 1, then 2 -- since Kubernetes always processes ordinals from lowest to highest for any StatefulSet operation.

Descending order -- the highest-numbered Pod (2) is updated first, and the controller waits for it to become Ready before moving to the next-lower ordinal, the reverse of the ascending order used for scale-up.
All Pods are updated simultaneously regardless of ordinal, since rolling updates use the Parallel pod management policy by default.
A random order chosen independently at the start of each rollout.
assessments.explanation: This concept is explicit that rolling updates 'follow the same descending-ordinal discipline' as scale-down -- the highest-numbered Pod is updated first, with the controller waiting for it to become Ready before proceeding to the next-lower ordinal -- which is deliberately 'the reverse of the ascending-ordinal order used for initial scale-up.' It's an easy point to get backwards by assuming update order mirrors creation order, which is exactly why this is worth testing directly. Options A, C, and D all describe orderings the default OrderedReady policy does not use for rolling updates.

assessments.prompt: A colleague asks why a 3-node distributed database can't just run as a Deployment with 3 replicas, given that a Deployment already handles self-healing and scaling. Explain, tying together identity, storage, and ordering, why all three of a StatefulSet's guarantees matter together for this specific kind of workload.
assessments.modelAnswer: A Deployment's self-healing and scaling are built entirely around the assumption that every replica is interchangeable -- any Pod can be deleted and replaced by an equivalent one with no meaningful difference, which is exactly true for a stateless web tier but false for a distributed database, where each node typically holds a distinct role or a distinct portion of the data and needs to be addressed specifically, not as 'any one of the pool.' A StatefulSet's three guarantees exist specifically to support that non-interchangeability, and they matter together rather than individually: stable ordinal identity (web-0, web-1, web-2, preserved across any replacement) means peers and clients can reliably address a *specific* member of the cluster by a name that doesn't change even after that member's Pod is replaced -- essential for something like 'always connect to node 0 as the primary' or a gossip protocol that expects to reach the same peer addresses over time. Stable per-replica storage via volumeClaimTemplates means that when node 1's Pod is replaced -- crash, node failure, routine rolling update -- the replacement reattaches to node 1's own specific data rather than starting from an empty volume or, worse, from a volume shared with a different node's Pod; without this, every Pod replacement in a Deployment-based attempt at the same thing would effectively wipe that node's contribution to the cluster's data, forcing an expensive resync from peers every single time, if the database software even supports that path robustly. Ordered, sequential creation and deletion matters for correctness during genuinely delicate moments -- a fresh cluster's first node bootstrapping before others try to join it, or a scale-down removing the most recently added, least-entrenched member first rather than an arbitrary one that might currently be the primary. Strip out any one of the three guarantees and the remaining two don't fully solve the problem: identity without storage means you can address 'node 1' reliably but it comes back empty every time; storage without identity means the right data exists somewhere but nothing gives peers a stable way to find the specific node holding it; either without ordering risks correctness issues during bootstrap and scale-down that a distributed system with quorum or leader-election logic genuinely cares about. That's why these three properties are bundled into a single controller rather than left as three separate features to combine yourself.
